name: Pan-Slavism
summary: Pan-Slavism is a nineteenth-century Romantic movement holding that the Slavic peoples share a language family, ancestry and culture and should stand together politically or culturally. It ranged from Austroslav federalism and equal national rights inside the Habsburg monarchy to Russian-led visions of a Slavic union under the Tsar, and from Prague liberals to Orthodox Slavophile conservatives. Its stated core is solidarity and self-determination for Slavs against German, Magyar and Ottoman domination.
scope: The nineteenth-century Pan-Slav movement as the reference works define it (Britannica s6, Encyclopedia of Modern Europe s7, Encyclopedia of Russian History s8, Encyclopedia of Ukraine s9): a movement that recognised a common ethnic background among the Slavs and sought to unite them for common cultural and political goals. It covers the Habsburg strand (Dobrovský, Kollár, Šafárik, Palacký, the 1848 Prague Slav Congress and its aim of a federation of equal peoples under Habsburg rule; Austro-Slavism), and the Russian strand of the 1860s on (Slavophile-influenced, a Russian-dominated Slav confederation; Danilevsky's Russia and Europe), with Križanić as precursor. Where strands conflict (federation versus Russian leadership, constitutionalism versus autocracy) answers are 0 or low. Later Yugoslavism, Soviet-era All-Slavic committees and modern Euro-Slavism are excluded, as are Slavophilism's own Orthodox and anti-Western doctrines except where the sources tie them to Pan-Slavism.

missingStatements.rationale: The Prague manifesto asked the Austrian emperor to turn the monarchy into a federation of nations with equal rights, and rejects dominance of one nation over another.

missingStatements.text: A people's shared language and culture is a sufficient basis for political solidarity across state borders.
missingStatements.rationale: Pan-Slavism rested on the Slavic languages' similarity and shared identity, built by philologists and folklorists, as the basis for unity.

notes: Strands diverge: the Habsburg strand (Palacký, the 1848 Prague congress) asked for a federation of equal nations with liberty and equal rights, while the Russian strand sought a Russian-led Slav confederation. Splits are 0 at low confidence. Answers rest only on the five reference works and the 1848 manifesto (Palacký, a key figure); the earlier answers that rested on Wikipedia, the Slavophile entries or inference were nulled. Slavophilism's own doctrines (Orthodoxy, autocracy, the commune) are a related movement's and were not used. Themes searched: nation and self-determination, federation and minorities, rights and privilege, war and conquest, religion, economy, government form, international order; the defining sources speak only to the national, minority, rights and expansion themes, so most dividing lines stay uncovered and the uncertainty rule is failed. Kohn's Pan-Slavism: Its History and Ideology has no free full text online.

keyFigures.role: Slovak poet whose Slávy dcera is the movement's chief literary expression
keyFigures.quote: Jan Kollár (1793–1852) wrote the sonnet cycle Daughter of Sláva (1824), the greatest literary expression of the Pan-Slav idea.

keyFigures.role: Slovak philologist who gave Pan-Slavism its scholarly basis
keyFigures.quote: The Czech philologist Pavel Jozef Safarik (1795 – 1861) and his friend, poet Jan Kollar, regarded the Slavs historically as one nation.

keyFigures.role: Czech historian who convened the 1848 Prague Slav Congress
keyFigures.quote: the Czech historian František Palacký convened a Slav congress in Prague

keyFigures.role: Slovak codifier of Slovak, a Pan-Slav who later changed his views
keyFigures.quote: Another Slovak, L'udovít Štúr (1815–1856), rejected Czech in favor of codifying a distinct Slovak tongue

keyFigures.role: Czech linguist whose codification of Czech underlay Habsburg Pan-Slavism
keyFigures.quote: Dobrovský (1753–1829), who codified Czech after more than a century of neglect, made Czech the main candidate for a unifying language.

keyFigures.role: Russian theorist of a Slavic union led by Russia
keyFigures.quote: Russia and Europe , by Nikolai Yakovlevich Danilevsky (1822 – 1885).

keyFigures.role: Seventeenth-century precursor urging a Slavic union under Russia
keyFigures.quote: Krizanic (1618 – 1683) is often regarded as a precursor of Panslavism because he urged the unification of all Slavs under the leadership of Russia and the Vatican.

keyWorks.title: Slávy dcera
keyWorks.author: Ján Kollár
keyWorks.quote: wrote the epic poem Slávy dcera (Slava's Daughter)

keyWorks.title: Russia and Europe
keyWorks.author: Nikolay Danilevsky
keyWorks.quote: As outlined in his Russia and Europe (1869), Danilevsky's aim was to unite all the countries and peoples who spoke Slavic languages on the grounds that they possessed common cultural, economic, and political goals.
